verdicts.reason: The core value claim is that OEMs, clouds and makers will trade a cash-settled DRAM contract and so supply liquidity. No evidence supports that, and the precedents point the other way. SGX announced the 'world's first DRAM futures' for 1Q, then 2Q, 2003 (contract cut from 10,000 to 1,000 pieces). Semicon Exchange and Semiconductor Futures Exchange tried the same in 2003, and CBOT, NYMEX and the Pacific Stock Exchange studied memory-chip futures in the late 1980s and early 1990s. No traded DRAM price contract surfaced in a 2026 search (Risk.net, Mondo Visione, EDN, via search snippets). The card itself concedes there is no settlement-grade index, and the incumbent hedge is physical LTAs that simply re-price. The only path below T3 is licensing an index to an existing exchange, and that collapses into C-86 (Memory Cost Escalation Index).

verdicts.reason: The venture's whole P&L is a short call on the DRAM contract price. Fair premium for a 12-month at-the-money cap is 16.7-20.7% of capped spend (Black-76 at 44-55% volatility; reproduced by hand: 2N(0.22)-1 = 17.4% before discounting). The 99th-percentile loss is $1.5-2.1M per $1M capped, so profit depends only on which way the price moves. Buyers self-select: they buy caps when they expect increases and skip them when they expect falls, so the product disappears in the 2028 turn. The allocation-guarantee leg needs physical stock the venture can only buy at spot (~1.7x contract), which is C-89's negative-EV trade. This is a financial bet on the cycle that needs a fronting insurer or swap dealer, not an operating business.

verdicts.reason: The lessor has no allocation, so it buys the same street-priced RDIMMs the lessee could buy (the model assumes $1,600 against $1,300 contract and $2,064 street). Its only product is money, and the named buyers already get that money more cheaply inside server-level financing. In 2026 CoreWeave closed an $8.5B A3-rated GPU-backed facility, Lambda a $926M Baa2 term loan (reported at about SOFR+3%), Nebius $775M, and Sharon AI $356M at 9.95% fixed, all at ~60-70% LTV (via search snippets). That is below the card's 14% lessor IRR, and these loans already fund the DRAM inside the servers. A memory-only lessor would therefore lose on $/GB-month, offer no supply security, and match cash-flow timing only at a higher price. It would also be left with the weakest credits that cannot raise GPU-backed debt. On top of that it holds peak-priced residuals into the glut (-29% to -58% IRR if lessees walk at months 18 or 12) and is exposed to a reported neocloud refinancing wall in 2026-28.

verdicts.reason: No kill rule applies. The DFARS mechanism is verified: this auditor opened 252.246-7008 and 246.870-2, which require contractors to buy first from OCMs, authorized suppliers or 'authorized aftermarket manufacturers'. Rochester proves the model at scale: the world's largest wafer bank (>10B die, expanding to ~30B), 'authorized by over 70' OCMs, and DRAM from SDRAM to DDR5 plus LPDDR4x through an Intelligent Memory partnership (via search snippets). So the business is possible and profitable, but for incumbents. The card's own model sells 90% of a bank in years 3-8, which pushes first revenue out, and whether any Winbond, ESMT, Etron or Nanya OCM would authorize a startup is STILL-UNVERIFIED. Score it low on capital, time to revenue, competition and founder fit rather than killing it.

verdicts.reason: The demand mechanism is verified (opened by this auditor). DFARS 252.246-7008(c)(2) makes the contractor 'responsible for inspection, testing, and authentication' when traceability fails, and FAR 52.246-26 treats used-as-new as counterfeit. The methods are routine (TRL 9), so no kill rule applies. The market is crowded, though, including inside the card's own East Coast corridor. SMT Corp in Sandy Hook CT holds ANAB ISO/IEC 17025 + AS6171 HRL2, is DLA QTSL-recognized and expanded to the UK in Dec 2025. Micross Clearwater FL is 17025/AS6171/AS6081 accredited with a RAM tester and offers full-lot AS6171 in about 2 weeks. A2 Global (FL), Vyrian (Houston) and White Horse Labs (Cleveland, DLA-approved) also compete (all via search snippets). Margin and time to revenue are optimistic: the card's 41% margin assumes 60 lots/month, 1.7x breakeven, while its own model shows -34% at 20 lots/month and 22% at 40.
